assumptions: The recorded start and end times bound the automated response only; they are not a measurement of how long the service was degraded, and the sub-second 'duration' should not be read as an outage length.
It is assumed but not verified that the HighErrorRate alert corresponds to a genuine condition on io-shop; an alerting or metrics-pipeline fault has not been ruled out.
Customer impact is unassessed, not confirmed absent — no data was available to judge it.
The single 'candidate cause' recorded is a statement that no cause was found, not a hypothesis with any supporting evidence.
input.executive_summary: An automated alert reported an elevated error rate on one of our services late on 15 September 2026. The automated responder picked the alert up immediately and tried to pull the service's recent performance data, but no data came back, so it could not tell what was happening, whether customers were affected, or how long any problem lasted. Nothing was changed or repaired; the incident was handed to a human on-call engineer with the note that there was not enough evidence to proceed. The open timestamps show only how long the automated attempt took, not how long any underlying problem existed. What went wrong, who it affected, and whether it is still happening are all still unknown and depend on the follow-up investigation. A separate question worth answering is why the metrics could not be read at all, since that gap is what stopped the response.
input.root_cause: Unknown. A HighErrorRate alert fired on io-shop, but the investigation retrieved zero minutes of metrics for the incident window (anchored on 22:56), so no cause was established and the incident was escalated for human investigation. No logs were read and no remediating actions were taken, so it is also unknown whether the alert reflected a real fault in io-shop or a problem in the metrics/alerting path itself.
